doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Chords, 'outside' playing and Coltrane
summary: Kirchner discusses naming chords in his scores and what playing outside means, citing Bill Watrous, Coltrane, Dave Liebman and Richie Beirach.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If I looked at a nonet score and I looked at beat one of measure four, like everybody’s playing, maybe like two or three beats, could I discern what the chord is for the most part, in your writing?

I suppose, I mean if you’re an educated musician like you are, yeah, I would imagine you could. Not all the time. I mean sometimes we just write things that — as Herbie Hancock said, we just, it’s hard to put names on these things, they’re just sounds.
You know. But I think for the most part you could come up with some kind of nomenclature that would describe what the chord was. But with some of the more outside things perhaps not.

What constitutes outside for you? I had this sort of a similar question I was going to bring up about the thought process in your head when you’re improvising. Bill Watrous said yeah you can play outside but you better know what you’re outside of, and you ought to be able to bring it back inside, or something like that.

Yeah. That’s a really great comment. Yeah, well the people who know what they’re doing, you know, like Coltrane would go outside, say Coltrane would play a tune like “Impressions” you know, like which is D minor and then E flat minor for the bridge. I mean he would go outside of the modes, outside of D minor for X amount of time, but his voice leading was so good that he would, you know, he would play outside of those basic modes but come back in after a certain point just to re-establish that he knew what he was doing and he knew how to create dissonance but he knew how to come back in to just obey the laws of good voice leading, let’s put it that way. I mean there are some people who I’ve heard play quote outside who really don’t know what they’re doing. They’re just playing notes that are deliberately dissonant just for the sense of creating dissonance but they really don’t understand the theory behind it. Like for example there’s a great book by Dave Liebman called A Chromatic Approach to Jazz Harmony and Melody, where it’s a book basically about how to play outside but with theoretical knowledge. And you know I mean he talks about things like that, he and Richie Beirach were pioneers in that kind of outside kind of playing but with really good theoretical knowledge. And those are people who know how to play outside but do so with — that it
makes musical sense. And there’s a logic to it, it’s not just haphazard or half-assed or, you know, there’s a musicality to it.
